analysis.one_liner: IndiGo (InterGlobe Aviation) is India's largest airline by passengers carried, running a low-cost domestic and international flight network.
analysis.whats_happening: Q2 FY27 results are due on 30 October 2026, about two weeks out. On 16 October 2026 the stock fell ~2.3% to ₹4,668.70 after the Centre told the Supreme Court that new rules to regulate airfares have been finalised and will be published within two weeks, with the case returning on 16 November 2026 - this stems from a PIL over 'arbitrary' pricing and cut baggage allowances filed after IndiGo's December 2025 scheduling crisis. The same day, IndiGo closed a $328 million financing deal for eight Airbus aircraft.
analysis.plain_terms: Passenger numbers and revenue are growing fast - a record 123 million flown in FY26, revenue up 20% year-on-year in the June 2026 quarter - but the company has still booked net losses in most recent quarters. The gap is mostly rupee depreciation hitting dollar-denominated aircraft lease obligations on paper, plus rising fuel and labour costs, not a lack of customers. On top of that, a December 2025 flight-cancellation crisis and now a government push to cap airfares add a layer of operational and regulatory risk sitting on top of an otherwise busy, growing airline.
analysis.quarters: Q4 FY26 (Jan-Mar26): revenue +1.3% YoY to ₹22,438 cr, but a net loss of ₹2,537 cr as forex losses swelled to ₹4,882 cr from ₹1,117 cr a year earlier; stripping out forex and exceptional items, the company said underlying PAT was a positive ₹1,921 cr. EBITDAR margin fell to 28.5% from 30.8%, yield fell 2.2%, passengers were down 1.1%. Full FY26: net loss of ₹2,393 cr despite a record 123 million passengers (+4%); MD Rahul Bhatia attributed the swing to 'exceptionally sharp rupee depreciation' and labour-law changes, not demand. Q1 FY27 (Apr-Jun26): revenue +20% YoY, but a net loss of ₹238 cr (vs profit of ₹2,176 cr a year ago) as fuel costs jumped 86% YoY and forex plus Middle East-conflict disruption weighed; load factor slipped to 83.3% from 84.6%. Treat the headline net-loss figures with caution - management's own ex-forex/ex-exceptional numbers, where disclosed, have stayed positive, which is the more comparable operating signal.
analysis.performance_read: The stock is 23.9% below its 20 August 2025 peak of ₹6,155.5, and down 20.3% over one year versus Nifty's -9.5% - a real, uncorrected-by-any-split price decline (no splits or demergers in this period, so nothing to add back). Zoom out and the picture flips: 3-year return of +80.6% and 5-year return of +128.7% both crush the Nifty's +16.8% and +25.3%. So this reads as a strong multi-year compounder giving back a chunk of gains over the last year on a string of forex losses, an operational crisis, and now regulatory overhang - not a structural collapse, but not a trivial pullback either.
analysis.valuation_read: A trailing P/E isn't usable here - TTM EPS is negative (roughly -₹124 to -125/share) because of the forex-driven losses described above, not operating weakness. On P/B the stock trades around 28-29x book, which looks expensive, but that's partly because years of losses have shrunk the equity base, mechanically inflating P/B - a small denominator, not necessarily a rich valuation. Separately, reported ROCE near 40% suggests the market is pricing the flying business on its capital efficiency and growth, treating the forex hit as a translation item on US-dollar aircraft obligations rather than a true earnings problem. Whether that bet is correct depends on the rupee and on how the airfare-cap rules land - not verified against primary filings, so treat these ratios as directional.
analysis.growth_read: Growth has been volume-led: record 123 million passengers in FY26 and 20% revenue growth in Q1 FY27 came from capacity additions, new aircraft and route expansion, not mainly fare increases - Q4 FY26 actually showed yield down 2.2% and passengers down 1.1%, a soft patch within the growth trend. Margins have moved the other way: EBITDAR margin compressed to 28.5% from 30.8% YoY, and fuel costs rose 86% YoY in the most recent quarter, so the growth is currently outrunning margin discipline rather than being reinforced by it.
analysis.health_read: The core business appears to generate cash reasonably well - reported ROCE near 40% - but reported profit keeps missing that because of large non-operating forex losses (₹4,882 cr in a single quarter) on dollar-denominated aircraft lease obligations, plus rising fuel and labour costs. This looks like financial/currency risk sitting on top of a healthy demand base, not a business-model problem - passenger traffic is at record highs. One caveat: airlines typically carry large aircraft lease liabilities under Ind AS 116 that may or may not be fully captured in a simple debt-to-equity figure (reported near 0.26) - not verified against the company's own balance sheet, so don't take that ratio as the full leverage picture.
analysis.ownership_read: Promoters hold 41.57%, split between InterGlobe Enterprises (~35.7%) and co-founder Rakesh Gangwal (~4.5%). Promoter pledge is 0%. The notable ownership story is Gangwal's steady exit - his stake has fallen from about 29.7% in June 2023 to roughly 4.5%-5.9% currently, a multi-year sell-down by a founder rather than a one-off trim. Institutional ownership is substantial: mutual funds ~24.3%, FIIs ~20.3%, other institutions ~7.6%, with public holding only ~6.2% as of mid-2026.
strengths: Record 123 million passengers carried in FY26 and 20% revenue growth in Q1 FY27 show demand and scale are intact
Reported ROCE of roughly 40% suggests the core flying operation remains capital-efficient when forex noise is excluded
Zero promoter pledge and a reported debt-to-equity of 0.26 indicate no distress signal at the promoter or headline balance-sheet level
3-year (+80.6%) and 5-year (+128.7%) shareholder returns remain well ahead of the Nifty despite the past year's drawdown
watchpoints: Recurring headline net losses (₹2,537 cr in Q4 FY26, ₹238 cr in Q1 FY27) driven largely by forex translation on USD-denominated aircraft obligations - a weaker rupee hits the P&L directly

December 2025 scheduling crisis: ~4,500 flights cancelled over 10 days from non-compliance with new DGCA pilot rest-hour rules, a ₹22.2 cr DGCA fine, a ₹50 cr bank guarantee requirement and over ₹24 cr in passenger compensation

Government airfare-pricing rules are finalised and due for publication within two weeks of 16 October 2026, with the Supreme Court case returning 16 November 2026 - a direct threat to pricing power that already moved the stock -2.3% in a day
EBITDAR margin compression (28.5% vs 30.8% YoY in Q4 FY26) and an 86% YoY jump in fuel costs (Q1 FY27) show real cost pressure beyond just currency effects
Co-founder Rakesh Gangwal's promoter stake has fallen from ~29.7% to ~4.5-5.9% over three years - a long founder exit worth tracking for pace and completion
analysis.one_thing: The Q2 FY27 results due 30 October 2026 - specifically whether ex-forex, ex-exceptional operating profit stays positive - combined with the actual text of the government's airfare-pricing rules due for publication around the same time, will show whether this is a currency-translation problem sitting on a healthy franchise or a deeper structural margin and regulatory squeeze.
analysis.data_notes: Q4 FY26, FY26 full-year and Q1 FY27 results cross-checked across Business Standard, Upstox, Kotak Neo and Angel One, which agree on headline numbers. Promoter holding (~41.57%) and zero pledge cross-checked via Trendlyne, Choice India and Tijori Finance. P/E, P/B, ROE, ROCE and debt-to-equity are sourced from third-party aggregators (not the company's primary filing) and are flagged as directional rather than verified - in particular, whether the reported debt-to-equity includes Ind AS 116 lease liabilities could not be confirmed. Dividend data supplied shows a ₹10/share payout in August 2025 but a TTM dividend of 0 as of October 2026, which is consistent (that payout falls outside the trailing 12 months), not a contradiction.
